dossier.deep_context:
# 1323 in 2025: Aurelia’s value depends on the alliance around it

The base dossier describes a compact tilting elevator, ground acquisition, a differential end effector and dedicated L1 work. That list does not explain why the package was useful. The deeper story concerns where mass and motion were placed, how transitions were controlled, how the robot was practiced, and how a highly capable scoring robot could rationally spend important matches doing a low-valued task. This supplement combines team replies from the release discussion with attributed match interpretation. It does not certify every configuration or CAD revision.

## Ground acquisition changes the source of the cycle, not only the pickup

The team credits Spectrum’s published funneling prototypes as direct input to its thinking. That is a specific lineage claim by the team, stronger than an observer noticing a resemblance. [Acknowledgment](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/212).

A ground collector becomes strategically powerful only when the rest of the system can exploit it. The human player has to deliver useful coral near the intended work area; the robot has to acquire it in more than one plausible orientation; the handoff must preserve control; and the scoring motion must finish before the next piece is needed. Reducing travel can expose a new bottleneck in transfer or joint motion. The agent should therefore compare complete acquisition-to-next-acquisition cycles rather than assume a floor pickup automatically halves cycle time.

The RoboReplay review ledger preserves a progression from early floor-supplied cycles to widespread field supply, then to L1 placement and algae security. These are dated observations and interpretations, not proof that 1323 invented each tactic first. The recap author explicitly does not claim to know the first inventor. Use that ledger to find the relevant discussion, then use team releases for mechanism construction and official records for scores.

## A differential needs a coordinate system and a recovery plan

In its controls explanation, the team describes two CANcoders and average/difference relationships for pitch and roll, with useful resolution through the range of motion. It also describes pain caused by a poor zeroing arrangement on the practice machine. [Encoder explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/218).

The transferable issue is not the encoder brand. Coupled actuation makes a light moving assembly possible, but makes calibration, limits and fault recovery part of the mechanism. If a team loses one joint reference, it needs to know which physical configurations are still safe. A robot that must disassemble a gearbox or trust an eyeballed pose after every power cycle can spend far more competition time recovering than its nominal mechanism speed saves.

The thread’s belt discussion also keeps packaging costs visible. The team reports more tension than expected and explains the role of belt construction and wrap. A later answer discusses the packaging that reduced wrap and the use of current/velocity when detecting a limit, while suggesting a larger pulley or changed path as a potential improvement. [Belt experience](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/242). [Packaging discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/250). Do not copy a thin, low-mass elevator rendering without the tension, stiffness, bearing loads and reference strategy that support it.

## Mechanically possible motion is not the same as permitted match motion

The team explains an emphasis on continuous joint motion toward useful states rather than a sequence of pauses. It also describes driver overrides for L1 and handoff behavior, a later allowance for algae-intake positioning, and Worlds changes including additional vision for L1 and default stow behavior. These are control-policy changes, not evidence that every physically reachable pose was always exposed to the driver. [Operating policy](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/236).

Another reply describes a superstructure state containing elevator position, elevator pivot and wrist pitch/roll, with a choreographer that builds safe transitions. A separate answer discusses using differential controller support once the mechanics and sensing were correct. [State representation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/283). [Controller/mechanical dependency](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/281).

An agent recommending this architecture should explicitly include that transition layer. A tilting elevator with a versatile wrist can have excellent final poses and still collide with its own intake during the path between them. The architecture should name which motions can overlap, which require a clearance condition, what the operator can interrupt, and where a stalled transition leaves the game piece. This is a reason to study code releases alongside CAD, while preserving their exact commit and event relevance. A public repository’s current default branch is not automatically the version run at a particular event.

## Human control remained part of the successful system

The team describes left/right branch selection relative to the nearest reef location and explains that manual release could be cleaner than a fully automatic release because of mechanism quirks. Driver and operator coordination also helped prevent intake interference with pipes. [Driver interface](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/303).

This avoids a common generalization error: a high-performing robot is not necessarily autonomous in every part of teleop. A deliberately manual action can be a reasonable way to handle ambiguous sensing or preserve operator judgment. The relevant measure is the entire decision-and-execution loop, including its error rate under contact and visual obstruction. The agent should not recommend automatic release merely because the mechanism has accurate joints. It should ask whether the observations needed to release safely are actually available.

## The build history includes abandoned mechanisms

The team’s timeline describes early CAD blocks, a largely functional machine by the following phase, and subsequent redesign. It names claw and hanger work, removal of suction, later mass reduction, a 2910-inspired hanger and Worlds emphasis on robustness and weight. [Development account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/263).

The abandoned suction matters. A database that gathers every impressive prototype and treats all of them as features of the final robot produces an impossible composite. The correct representation is a versioned choice: a concept existed, a later report says it was removed, and the final package must be determined from the dated sources. Similarly, “2910 hanger” is a lineage lead that still needs the year and exact retained principles. It is not permission to assume identical dimensions or identical integration into a different superstructure.

## Practice and material selection are part of the architecture’s cost

The team describes building the practice robot early enough for extensive validation, while the competition machine was completed much closer to its event. It also notes configuration drift between two robots as a cost. [Two-robot account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/267). A later reply gives a rough team estimate about the benefit of their practice time; this is a self-assessment, not a controlled measurement or a universal hours-to-performance equation. [Practice reflection](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/305).

Another reply contrasts inexpensive, quickly iterated practice prints with competition material chosen for confidence, while noting that practice hardware accumulated more hours. [Printing experience](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/327). Material choice therefore has to be read with the test exposure, replacement cadence and failure consequence. A competition material does not by itself explain the success of the mechanism; rapid cheap prototypes may have discovered the load path and geometry that made the final part straightforward.

## Why specializing in L1 can be the correct job for an excellent robot

Once partners can reliably fill the higher branches, an additional robot’s ability to place another L4 has little immediate value unless it frees a partner for a better job. Fast L1 acquisition and controlled placement can instead increase the alliance’s remaining score. Orientation and release geometry affect how densely coral can be arranged near a convenient face, which changes how soon the robot must move to a less convenient face. This is an alliance-dependent marginal-value argument, not a claim that L1 is intrinsically the best task.

The RoboReplay finals analysis attributes importance to 1323’s L1 stacking and 2910’s algae steals. It also interprets score visibility and drive-team decisions; those psychological explanations remain commentary. See the complete review of `SQure1sSDpk` in the RoboReplay ledger for the source, with official Einstein records used for scores. A future agent should preserve the difference between the visible configuration, a measured cycle count, a team statement about its plan and an analyst’s explanation of the result.

## What to borrow and what to test

Retrieve this case for low moving mass, coupled joints, bidirectional scoring, dedicated L1 placement and the distinction between capability and match role. Test the collection/handoff cycle with delivered coral at realistic locations, joints moving simultaneously, contact during acquisition, worn components and an interrupted transition. Validate zeroing and recovery as deliberately as scoring. Pair the case with 2910’s arm architecture and 1690’s low-mass vacuum/differential system to compare where each design puts its complexity. The agent should state which capability your likely PCH partners supply; without that assumption, a recommendation to optimize L1 may copy the visible job while missing the alliance that made it valuable.


# 2025-1323: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## AURELIA: package the base around two different clearances

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p4](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=4) · [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=5)

**Published construction:** 28-inch square chassis; X2i elevator-side modules and X2t intake-side modules; custom lowering spacers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Motor protection, low chassis and intake gearbox clearance.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Choosing different module orientations within one drivebase is a packaging solution rather than a reason to recommend mixed modules universally. A motor placed inside can protect the elevator-side envelope while an outward placement can free an intake drive path. The lowering hardware must preserve module stiffness and ground clearance under a loaded, accelerating robot. Low mass is helpful, but the more relevant quantity for fast reef approach is the loaded center of mass and its motion as the shoulder and elevator change state. Include bumper and battery interfaces in the same model.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Sweep the complete intake/elevator envelope against each module; measure clearance and wheel unloading through aggressive scoring transitions.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## AURELIA: separate coral and algae contacts on a shared axis

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=8) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=9) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/131)

**Published construction:** Coaxial intake pivots; separate deployment reductions; shared roller drive; bilateral transfer tubes.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** The team explicitly ties this intake choice to horizontal L1 placement, alongside concerns about a separate centering/indexing system.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Sharing an axis does not make these one generic intake. Each piece needs a different contact geometry, and the dedicated L1 action depends on their relative positions. Driving both sides helps prevent an arm from twisting out of phase during asymmetric contact. A common roller drive saves a motor and packaging but couples the desired surface speeds of the two pickup functions. The useful retrieval target is the entire relative geometry and state sequence: which surface acquires, which guides, and which constrains the coral during release. A lone roller photo cannot explain the L1 performance.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Film the complete L1 cycle from first floor contact through release; vary coral orientation, reef occupancy and approach angle.

**Limits:** Team reply reports difficult horizontal approaches beyond about 45 degrees, extensive practice and late-season durability work. Successful match execution is not proof of effortless any-orientation pickup.

## AURELIA: center coral before a direct handoff

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=9)

**Published construction:** Flex upper rollers, grippy lower rollers, about 0.125-inch coral compression and proximity detection.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Center coral and hand directly into the end effector.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A low-compression pickup can reduce the force required to accept an awkwardly oriented tube, but it leaves less traction margin when the surfaces are dirty or the coral is wedged against another piece. Centering before transfer reduces the number of states the end effector must solve. A direct handoff avoids an intermediate tray, while demanding that the receiving geometry arrive at the right position before the piece loses its previous constraint. Sensor placement should identify the handoff state, rather than simply report that some portion of a long tube is nearby.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test slow, diagonal and multi-piece approaches; observe whether detection occurs before, during or after reliable ownership transfers.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## AURELIA: four-stage lift on a rotating shoulder

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=6) · [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=10) · [PDF p11](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=11)

**Published construction:** Shoulder-supported four-stage continuous elevator; internal HTD belts; interlocking extended-stage stops.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Compact packaging with stiffness at scoring height.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The shoulder changes both the lift’s direction and its center-of-mass path. A multi-stage lift can reach high while stowing short, but introduces more interfaces that can deflect or develop play. Hard stops that engage at extension can add stiffness where the mechanism otherwise has the least overlap; they must not produce damaging impacts at operating speed. The carriage’s integrated gearbox reduces redundant structure while making belt access and service sequencing important. In the alliance role described by the user, much of the robot’s value comes from low scoring and algae, yet its high reach still supplies capability and tactical flexibility.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure tip error and settling after shoulder/elevator transitions, including side acceleration and partial rather than only full extension.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## AURELIA: differential wrist and independently driven rollers

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p12](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=12) · [PDF p13](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=13)

**Published construction:** Printed bevel differential; paired 61.6:1 drives; independent coral rollers; front algae pinch wheels.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reorient coral while keeping the moving end effector compact.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A differential combines two motor coordinates into two output motions. That can package orientation control densely, but means a joint motion may require both motors and leave less authority for the other axis at the same instant. Printed bevel gears need controlled bearing alignment and a stiffness model; backlash at a small output stage becomes placement error at the coral tip. Independent roller contacts can change tube orientation before release, which is particularly valuable for intentional L1 placement and stacking. The same hardware can support very different alliance jobs, so high-level capability must be separated from the task actually assigned in a match.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Command combined wrist motions under realistic piece load; measure output backlash and horizontal-coral placement consistency across L1 pile heights.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## AURELIA: reuse the shoulder and reposition the cage

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=8) · [PDF p14](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=14)

**Published construction:** Powered cage capture, passive latches, sliding support and shoulder-driven lifting; algae intake supplies support.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reuse primary joints while controlling the hanging geometry.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A shared-joint climb saves dedicated structure only if the primary system can react the new loads. Capturing one cage tube is different from supporting the robot after the cage rotates; the lower reaction point and position of the chain relative to the robot’s center of mass determine the motion. The sliding support permits that geometry to change rather than requiring a single fixed pivot to solve every phase. Reuse also couples faults: a damaged shoulder, end effector or intake latch can affect climb. Record the support contact explicitly instead of reducing the design to “uses its arm to climb.”

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test cage swing and off-center capture, inspect every reaction contact, and verify retention after power is removed.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

dossier.narrative_context:
# 1323 in 2025: Aurelia’s value depends on the alliance around it

The base dossier describes a compact tilting elevator, ground acquisition, a differential end effector and dedicated L1 work. That list does not explain why the package was useful. The deeper story concerns where mass and motion were placed, how transitions were controlled, how the robot was practiced, and how a highly capable scoring robot could rationally spend important matches doing a low-valued task. This supplement combines team replies from the release discussion with attributed match interpretation. It does not certify every configuration or CAD revision.

## Ground acquisition changes the source of the cycle, not only the pickup

The team credits Spectrum’s published funneling prototypes as direct input to its thinking. That is a specific lineage claim by the team, stronger than an observer noticing a resemblance. [Acknowledgment](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/212).

A ground collector becomes strategically powerful only when the rest of the system can exploit it. The human player has to deliver useful coral near the intended work area; the robot has to acquire it in more than one plausible orientation; the handoff must preserve control; and the scoring motion must finish before the next piece is needed. Reducing travel can expose a new bottleneck in transfer or joint motion. The agent should therefore compare complete acquisition-to-next-acquisition cycles rather than assume a floor pickup automatically halves cycle time.

The RoboReplay review ledger preserves a progression from early floor-supplied cycles to widespread field supply, then to L1 placement and algae security. These are dated observations and interpretations, not proof that 1323 invented each tactic first. The recap author explicitly does not claim to know the first inventor. Use that ledger to find the relevant discussion, then use team releases for mechanism construction and official records for scores.

## A differential needs a coordinate system and a recovery plan

In its controls explanation, the team describes two CANcoders and average/difference relationships for pitch and roll, with useful resolution through the range of motion. It also describes pain caused by a poor zeroing arrangement on the practice machine. [Encoder explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/218).

The transferable issue is not the encoder brand. Coupled actuation makes a light moving assembly possible, but makes calibration, limits and fault recovery part of the mechanism. If a team loses one joint reference, it needs to know which physical configurations are still safe. A robot that must disassemble a gearbox or trust an eyeballed pose after every power cycle can spend far more competition time recovering than its nominal mechanism speed saves.

The thread’s belt discussion also keeps packaging costs visible. The team reports more tension than expected and explains the role of belt construction and wrap. A later answer discusses the packaging that reduced wrap and the use of current/velocity when detecting a limit, while suggesting a larger pulley or changed path as a potential improvement. [Belt experience](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/242). [Packaging discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/250). Do not copy a thin, low-mass elevator rendering without the tension, stiffness, bearing loads and reference strategy that support it.

## Mechanically possible motion is not the same as permitted match motion

The team explains an emphasis on continuous joint motion toward useful states rather than a sequence of pauses. It also describes driver overrides for L1 and handoff behavior, a later allowance for algae-intake positioning, and Worlds changes including additional vision for L1 and default stow behavior. These are control-policy changes, not evidence that every physically reachable pose was always exposed to the driver. [Operating policy](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/236).

Another reply describes a superstructure state containing elevator position, elevator pivot and wrist pitch/roll, with a choreographer that builds safe transitions. A separate answer discusses using differential controller support once the mechanics and sensing were correct. [State representation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/283). [Controller/mechanical dependency](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/281).

An agent recommending this architecture should explicitly include that transition layer. A tilting elevator with a versatile wrist can have excellent final poses and still collide with its own intake during the path between them. The architecture should name which motions can overlap, which require a clearance condition, what the operator can interrupt, and where a stalled transition leaves the game piece. This is a reason to study code releases alongside CAD, while preserving their exact commit and event relevance. A public repository’s current default branch is not automatically the version run at a particular event.

## Human control remained part of the successful system

The team describes left/right branch selection relative to the nearest reef location and explains that manual release could be cleaner than a fully automatic release because of mechanism quirks. Driver and operator coordination also helped prevent intake interference with pipes. [Driver interface](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/303).

This avoids a common generalization error: a high-performing robot is not necessarily autonomous in every part of teleop. A deliberately manual action can be a reasonable way to handle ambiguous sensing or preserve operator judgment. The relevant measure is the entire decision-and-execution loop, including its error rate under contact and visual obstruction. The agent should not recommend automatic release merely because the mechanism has accurate joints. It should ask whether the observations needed to release safely are actually available.

## The build history includes abandoned mechanisms

The team’s timeline describes early CAD blocks, a largely functional machine by the following phase, and subsequent redesign. It names claw and hanger work, removal of suction, later mass reduction, a 2910-inspired hanger and Worlds emphasis on robustness and weight. [Development account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/263).

The abandoned suction matters. A database that gathers every impressive prototype and treats all of them as features of the final robot produces an impossible composite. The correct representation is a versioned choice: a concept existed, a later report says it was removed, and the final package must be determined from the dated sources. Similarly, “2910 hanger” is a lineage lead that still needs the year and exact retained principles. It is not permission to assume identical dimensions or identical integration into a different superstructure.

## Practice and material selection are part of the architecture’s cost

The team describes building the practice robot early enough for extensive validation, while the competition machine was completed much closer to its event. It also notes configuration drift between two robots as a cost. [Two-robot account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/267). A later reply gives a rough team estimate about the benefit of their practice time; this is a self-assessment, not a controlled measurement or a universal hours-to-performance equation. [Practice reflection](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/305).

Another reply contrasts inexpensive, quickly iterated practice prints with competition material chosen for confidence, while noting that practice hardware accumulated more hours. [Printing experience](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/327). Material choice therefore has to be read with the test exposure, replacement cadence and failure consequence. A competition material does not by itself explain the success of the mechanism; rapid cheap prototypes may have discovered the load path and geometry that made the final part straightforward.

## Why specializing in L1 can be the correct job for an excellent robot

Once partners can reliably fill the higher branches, an additional robot’s ability to place another L4 has little immediate value unless it frees a partner for a better job. Fast L1 acquisition and controlled placement can instead increase the alliance’s remaining score. Orientation and release geometry affect how densely coral can be arranged near a convenient face, which changes how soon the robot must move to a less convenient face. This is an alliance-dependent marginal-value argument, not a claim that L1 is intrinsically the best task.

The RoboReplay finals analysis attributes importance to 1323’s L1 stacking and 2910’s algae steals. It also interprets score visibility and drive-team decisions; those psychological explanations remain commentary. See the complete review of `SQure1sSDpk` in the RoboReplay ledger for the source, with official Einstein records used for scores. A future agent should preserve the difference between the visible configuration, a measured cycle count, a team statement about its plan and an analyst’s explanation of the result.

## What to borrow and what to test

Retrieve this case for low moving mass, coupled joints, bidirectional scoring, dedicated L1 placement and the distinction between capability and match role. Test the collection/handoff cycle with delivered coral at realistic locations, joints moving simultaneously, contact during acquisition, worn components and an interrupted transition. Validate zeroing and recovery as deliberately as scoring. Pair the case with 2910’s arm architecture and 1690’s low-mass vacuum/differential system to compare where each design puts its complexity. The agent should state which capability your likely PCH partners supply; without that assumption, a recommendation to optimize L1 may copy the visible job while missing the alliance that made it valuable.

technical_notes.title: AURELIA: package the base around two different clearances
technical_notes.construction: 28-inch square chassis; X2i elevator-side modules and X2t intake-side modules; custom lowering spacers.
technical_notes.team_stated_reason: Motor protection, low chassis and intake gearbox clearance.
technical_notes.engineering_analysis: Choosing different module orientations within one drivebase is a packaging solution rather than a reason to recommend mixed modules universally. A motor placed inside can protect the elevator-side envelope while an outward placement can free an intake drive path. The lowering hardware must preserve module stiffness and ground clearance under a loaded, accelerating robot. Low mass is helpful, but the more relevant quantity for fast reef approach is the loaded center of mass and its motion as the shoulder and elevator change state. Include bumper and battery interfaces in the same model.
technical_notes.recommended_validation: Sweep the complete intake/elevator envelope against each module; measure clearance and wheel unloading through aggressive scoring transitions.
technical_notes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technical_notes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technical_notes.title: AURELIA: separate coral and algae contacts on a shared axis
technical_notes.construction: Coaxial intake pivots; separate deployment reductions; shared roller drive; bilateral transfer tubes.
technical_notes.team_stated_reason: The team explicitly ties this intake choice to horizontal L1 placement, alongside concerns about a separate centering/indexing system.
technical_notes.engineering_analysis: Sharing an axis does not make these one generic intake. Each piece needs a different contact geometry, and the dedicated L1 action depends on their relative positions. Driving both sides helps prevent an arm from twisting out of phase during asymmetric contact. A common roller drive saves a motor and packaging but couples the desired surface speeds of the two pickup functions. The useful retrieval target is the entire relative geometry and state sequence: which surface acquires, which guides, and which constrains the coral during release. A lone roller photo cannot explain the L1 performance.
technical_notes.recommended_validation: Film the complete L1 cycle from first floor contact through release; vary coral orientation, reef occupancy and approach angle.
technical_notes.limitations: Team reply reports difficult horizontal approaches beyond about 45 degrees, extensive practice and late-season durability work. Successful match execution is not proof of effortless any-orientation pickup.
technical_notes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technical_notes.title: AURELIA: center coral before a direct handoff
technical_notes.construction: Flex upper rollers, grippy lower rollers, about 0.125-inch coral compression and proximity detection.
technical_notes.team_stated_reason: Center coral and hand directly into the end effector.
technical_notes.engineering_analysis: A low-compression pickup can reduce the force required to accept an awkwardly oriented tube, but it leaves less traction margin when the surfaces are dirty or the coral is wedged against another piece. Centering before transfer reduces the number of states the end effector must solve. A direct handoff avoids an intermediate tray, while demanding that the receiving geometry arrive at the right position before the piece loses its previous constraint. Sensor placement should identify the handoff state, rather than simply report that some portion of a long tube is nearby.
technical_notes.recommended_validation: Test slow, diagonal and multi-piece approaches; observe whether detection occurs before, during or after reliable ownership transfers.
technical_notes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technical_notes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technical_notes.title: AURELIA: four-stage lift on a rotating shoulder
technical_notes.construction: Shoulder-supported four-stage continuous elevator; internal HTD belts; interlocking extended-stage stops.
technical_notes.team_stated_reason: Compact packaging with stiffness at scoring height.
technical_notes.engineering_analysis: The shoulder changes both the lift’s direction and its center-of-mass path. A multi-stage lift can reach high while stowing short, but introduces more interfaces that can deflect or develop play. Hard stops that engage at extension can add stiffness where the mechanism otherwise has the least overlap; they must not produce damaging impacts at operating speed. The carriage’s integrated gearbox reduces redundant structure while making belt access and service sequencing important. In the alliance role described by the user, much of the robot’s value comes from low scoring and algae, yet its high reach still supplies capability and tactical flexibility.
technical_notes.recommended_validation: Measure tip error and settling after shoulder/elevator transitions, including side acceleration and partial rather than only full extension.
technical_notes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technical_notes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technical_notes.title: AURELIA: differential wrist and independently driven rollers
technical_notes.construction: Printed bevel differential; paired 61.6:1 drives; independent coral rollers; front algae pinch wheels.
technical_notes.team_stated_reason: Reorient coral while keeping the moving end effector compact.
technical_notes.engineering_analysis: A differential combines two motor coordinates into two output motions. That can package orientation control densely, but means a joint motion may require both motors and leave less authority for the other axis at the same instant. Printed bevel gears need controlled bearing alignment and a stiffness model; backlash at a small output stage becomes placement error at the coral tip. Independent roller contacts can change tube orientation before release, which is particularly valuable for intentional L1 placement and stacking. The same hardware can support very different alliance jobs, so high-level capability must be separated from the task actually assigned in a match.
technical_notes.recommended_validation: Command combined wrist motions under realistic piece load; measure output backlash and horizontal-coral placement consistency across L1 pile heights.
technical_notes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technical_notes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technical_notes.title: AURELIA: reuse the shoulder and reposition the cage
technical_notes.construction: Powered cage capture, passive latches, sliding support and shoulder-driven lifting; algae intake supplies support.
technical_notes.team_stated_reason: Reuse primary joints while controlling the hanging geometry.
technical_notes.engineering_analysis: A shared-joint climb saves dedicated structure only if the primary system can react the new loads. Capturing one cage tube is different from supporting the robot after the cage rotates; the lower reaction point and position of the chain relative to the robot’s center of mass determine the motion. The sliding support permits that geometry to change rather than requiring a single fixed pivot to solve every phase. Reuse also couples faults: a damaged shoulder, end effector or intake latch can affect climb. Record the support contact explicitly instead of reducing the design to “uses its arm to climb.”
technical_notes.recommended_validation: Test cage swing and off-center capture, inspect every reaction contact, and verify retention after power is removed.
technical_notes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

It also describes pain caused by a poor zeroing arrangement on the practice machine. [Encoder explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/218).

The transferable issue is not the encoder brand. Coupled actuation makes a light moving assembly possible, but makes calibration, limits and fault recovery part of the mechanism. If a team loses one joint reference, it needs to know which physical configurations are still safe. A robot that must disassemble a gearbox or trust an eyeballed pose after every power cycle can spend far more competition time recovering than its nominal mechanism speed saves.

The thread’s belt discussion also keeps packaging costs visible. The team reports more tension than expected and explains the role of belt construction and wrap. A later answer discusses the packaging that reduced wrap and the use of current/velocity when detecting a limit, while suggesting a larger pulley or changed path as a potential improvement. [Belt experience](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/242). [Packaging discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/250). Do not copy a thin, low-mass elevator rendering without the tension, stiffness, bearing loads and reference strategy that support it.

## Mechanically possible motion is not the same as permitted match motion

The team explains an emphasis on continuous joint motion toward useful states rather than a sequence of pauses. It also describes driver overrides for L1 and handoff behavior, a later allowance for algae-intake positioning, and Worlds changes including additional vision for L1 and default stow behavior. These are control-policy changes, not evidence that every physically reachable pose was always exposed to the driver. [Operating policy](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/236).

Another reply describes a superstructure state containing elevator position, elevator pivot and wrist pitch/roll, with a choreographer that builds safe transitions. A separate answer discusses using differential controller support once the mechanics and sensing were correct. [State representation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/283). [Controller/mechanical dependency](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/281).

An agent recommending this architecture should explicitly include that transition layer. A tilting elevator with a versatile wrist can have excellent final poses and still collide with its own intake during the path between them. The architecture should name which motions can overlap, which require a clearance condition, what the operator can interrupt, and where a stalled transition leaves the game piece. This is a reason to study code releases alongside CAD, while preserving their exact commit and event relevance. A public repository’s current default branch is not automatically the version run at a particular event.

## Human control remained part of the successful system

The team describes left/right branch selection relative to the nearest reef location and explains that manual release could be cleaner than a fully automatic release because of mechanism quirks. Driver and operator coordination also helped prevent intake interference with pipes. [Driver interface](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/303).

This avoids a common generalization error: a high-performing robot is not necessarily autonomous in every part of teleop. A deliberately manual action can be a reasonable way to handle ambiguous sensing or preserve operator judgment. The relevant measure is the entire decision-and-execution loop, including its error rate under contact and visual obstruction. The agent should not recommend automatic release merely because the mechanism has accurate joints. It should ask whether the observations needed to release safely are actually available.

## The build history includes abandoned mechanisms

The team’s timeline describes early CAD blocks, a largely functional machine by the following phase, and subsequent redesign. It names claw and hanger work, removal of suction, later mass reduction, a 2910-inspired hanger and Worlds emphasis on robustness and weight. [Development account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/263).

The abandoned suction matters. A database that gathers every impressive prototype and treats all of them as features of the final robot produces an impossible composite. The correct representation is a versioned choice: a concept existed, a later report says it was removed, and the final package must be determined from the dated sources. Similarly, “2910 hanger” is a lineage lead that still needs the year and exact retained principles. It is not permission to assume identical dimensions or identical integration into a different superstructure.

## Practice and material selection are part of the architecture’s cost

The team describes building the practice robot early enough for extensive validation, while the competition machine was completed much closer to its event. It also notes configuration drift between two robots as a cost. [Two-robot account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/267). A later reply gives a rough team estimate about the benefit of their practice time; this is a self-assessment, not a controlled measurement or a universal hours-to-performance equation. [Practice reflection](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/305).

Another reply contrasts inexpensive, quickly iterated practice prints with competition material chosen for confidence, while noting that practice hardware accumulated more hours. [Printing experience](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/327). Material choice therefore has to be read with the test exposure, replacement cadence and failure consequence. A competition material does not by itself explain the success of the mechanism; rapid cheap prototypes may have discovered the load path and geometry that made the final part straightforward.

## Why specializing in L1 can be the correct job for an excellent robot

Once partners can reliably fill the higher branches, an additional robot’s ability to place another L4 has little immediate value unless it frees a partner for a better job. Fast L1 acquisition and controlled placement can instead increase the alliance’s remaining score. Orientation and release geometry affect how densely coral can be arranged near a convenient face, which changes how soon the robot must move to a less convenient face. This is an alliance-dependent marginal-value argument, not a claim that L1 is intrinsically the best task.

The RoboReplay finals analysis attributes importance to 1323’s L1 stacking and 2910’s algae steals. It also interprets score visibility and drive-team decisions; those psychological explanations remain commentary. See the complete review of `SQure1sSDpk` in the RoboReplay ledger for the source, with official Einstein records used for scores. A future agent should preserve the difference between the visible configuration, a measured cycle count, a team statement about its plan and an analyst’s explanation of the result.

## What to borrow and what to test

Retrieve this case for low moving mass, coupled joints, bidirectional scoring, dedicated L1 placement and the distinction between capability and match role. Test the collection/handoff cycle with delivered coral at realistic locations, joints moving simultaneously, contact during acquisition, worn components and an interrupted transition. Validate zeroing and recovery as deliberately as scoring. Pair the case with 2910’s arm architecture and 1690’s low-mass vacuum/differential system to compare where each design puts its complexity. The agent should state which capability your likely PCH partners supply; without that assumption, a recommendation to optimize L1 may copy the visible job while missing the alliance that made it valuable.

> Physical evidence update 2026-11-07: read the complete [upgrade report](../PHYSICAL_UPGRADE_REPORT.md) and the new physical studies in `data/physical_studies.jsonl`. Earlier source accounts below retain their publication scopes.

# 2025-1323: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## AURELIA: package the base around two different clearances

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p4](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=4) · [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=5)

**Published construction:** 28-inch square chassis; X2i elevator-side modules and X2t intake-side modules; custom lowering spacers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Motor protection, low chassis and intake gearbox clearance.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Choosing different module orientations within one drivebase is a packaging solution rather than a reason to recommend mixed modules universally. A motor placed inside can protect the elevator-side envelope while an outward placement can free an intake drive path. The lowering hardware must preserve module stiffness and ground clearance under a loaded, accelerating robot. Low mass is helpful, but the more relevant quantity for fast reef approach is the loaded center of mass and its motion as the shoulder and elevator change state. Include bumper and battery interfaces in the same model.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Sweep the complete intake/elevator envelope against each module; measure clearance and wheel unloading through aggressive scoring transitions.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## AURELIA: separate coral and algae contacts on a shared axis

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=8) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=9) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/131)

**Published construction:** Coaxial intake pivots; separate deployment reductions; shared roller drive; bilateral transfer tubes.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** The team explicitly ties this intake choice to horizontal L1 placement, alongside concerns about a separate centering/indexing system.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Sharing an axis does not make these one generic intake. Each piece needs a different contact geometry, and the dedicated L1 action depends on their relative positions. Driving both sides helps prevent an arm from twisting out of phase during asymmetric contact. A common roller drive saves a motor and packaging but couples the desired surface speeds of the two pickup functions. The useful retrieval target is the entire relative geometry and state sequence: which surface acquires, which guides, and which constrains the coral during release. A lone roller photo cannot explain the L1 performance.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Film the complete L1 cycle from first floor contact through release; vary coral orientation, reef occupancy and approach angle.

**Limits:** Team reply reports difficult horizontal approaches beyond about 45 degrees, extensive practice and late-season durability work. Successful match execution is not proof of effortless any-orientation pickup.

## AURELIA: center coral before a direct handoff

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=9)

**Published construction:** Flex upper rollers, grippy lower rollers, about 0.125-inch coral compression and proximity detection.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Center coral and hand directly into the end effector.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A low-compression pickup can reduce the force required to accept an awkwardly oriented tube, but it leaves less traction margin when the surfaces are dirty or the coral is wedged against another piece. Centering before transfer reduces the number of states the end effector must solve. A direct handoff avoids an intermediate tray, while demanding that the receiving geometry arrive at the right position before the piece loses its previous constraint. Sensor placement should identify the handoff state, rather than simply report that some portion of a long tube is nearby.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test slow, diagonal and multi-piece approaches; observe whether detection occurs before, during or after reliable ownership transfers.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## AURELIA: four-stage lift on a rotating shoulder

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=6) · [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=10) · [PDF p11](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=11)

**Published construction:** Shoulder-supported four-stage continuous elevator; internal HTD belts; interlocking extended-stage stops.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Compact packaging with stiffness at scoring height.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The shoulder changes both the lift’s direction and its center-of-mass path. A multi-stage lift can reach high while stowing short, but introduces more interfaces that can deflect or develop play. Hard stops that engage at extension can add stiffness where the mechanism otherwise has the least overlap; they must not produce damaging impacts at operating speed. The carriage’s integrated gearbox reduces redundant structure while making belt access and service sequencing important. In the alliance role described by the user, much of the robot’s value comes from low scoring and algae, yet its high reach still supplies capability and tactical flexibility.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure tip error and settling after shoulder/elevator transitions, including side acceleration and partial rather than only full extension.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## AURELIA: differential wrist and independently driven rollers

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p12](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=12) · [PDF p13](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=13)

**Published construction:** Printed bevel differential; paired 61.6:1 drives; independent coral rollers; front algae pinch wheels.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reorient coral while keeping the moving end effector compact.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A differential combines two motor coordinates into two output motions. That can package orientation control densely, but means a joint motion may require both motors and leave less authority for the other axis at the same instant. Printed bevel gears need controlled bearing alignment and a stiffness model; backlash at a small output stage becomes placement error at the coral tip. Independent roller contacts can change tube orientation before release, which is particularly valuable for intentional L1 placement and stacking. The same hardware can support very different alliance jobs, so high-level capability must be separated from the task actually assigned in a match.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Command combined wrist motions under realistic piece load; measure output backlash and horizontal-coral placement consistency across L1 pile heights.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## AURELIA: reuse the shoulder and reposition the cage

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=8) · [PDF p14](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=14)

**Published construction:** Powered cage capture, passive latches, sliding support and shoulder-driven lifting; algae intake supplies support.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reuse primary joints while controlling the hanging geometry.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A shared-joint climb saves dedicated structure only if the primary system can react the new loads. Capturing one cage tube is different from supporting the robot after the cage rotates; the lower reaction point and position of the chain relative to the robot’s center of mass determine the motion. The sliding support permits that geometry to change rather than requiring a single fixed pivot to solve every phase. Reuse also couples faults: a damaged shoulder, end effector or intake latch can affect climb. Record the support contact explicitly instead of reducing the design to “uses its arm to climb.”

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test cage swing and off-center capture, inspect every reaction contact, and verify retention after power is removed.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Drive | 6.48:1; 16.1-ft/s free; X60/X44 | [Source p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=5) |
| Shoulder | 182.25:1 per X44 drive | [Source p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=6) |
| Intake deploy | algae 64:1; coral 42.67:1 | [Source p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=7) |
| Lift | 6.875:1; one X60; two internal 18-mm HTD belts | [Source p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=10) |
| Differential | 61.6:1 per drive; #25H output chain | [Source p12](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=12) |
| End rollers | vertical X44 3:1; front 3-in wheels | [Source p13](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=13) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

# 2025-1323: AURELIA binder plus team sensor replies

Generated from `data/physical_studies.jsonl`; edit that authoritative record.

## Whole robot and packaging

The ground pickup spans the front of the base. Coral and algae mechanisms share an axis but have distinct contacts and drives. A central shoulder turns a four-stage elevator supported by an A-frame tied into the base; the carriage carries a compact differential wrist and two-piece end effector. The elevator changes both height and fore-aft position because its whole mast pivots. High scoring therefore sweeps a volume above and across the base, while ground intake deployment occupies the front. The base uses different module clearances fore and aft. Published stage and shoulder renders establish subassembly construction, but battery location, complete wire routing and removal operations remain incomplete.

## Piece flow

For coral, floor rollers catch and center the tube, then lift it into a direct handoff. The receiving end effector must be positioned before the donor releases its constraint. The elevator/shoulder move the retained tube to height; the differential reorients it while separate rollers manage placement and release. Algae follows its own intake contacts into the shared end effector, or is acquired from the reef. Climbing changes the force path: cage capture and support contacts allow the shoulder to lift the chassis rather than just a piece.

## Annotated views

Editorial reconstruction. Not to scale; only explicit dimension labels are source dimensions. No CAD-derived measurements. Dashed envelopes are schematic and not clearance certification.

![physical-2025-1323-transition](../../images/physical/physical-2025-1323-transition.png)

## Ground capture, orientation and direct handoff

### Published construction

The binder describes flex upper contacts, grippy lower rollers and roughly 0.125-inch coral compression. The original figure shows the wheel row, lower tube, side supports and deployment transmission.

### Team rationale / attribution boundary

Read cited historical note for team rationale; the operating reconstruction below is editorial and does not establish additional team intent.

### Editorial operating reconstruction

Catch the floor tube, center it between the contact regions, lift the intake, and meet the receiving wrist. The team reply identifies a diffuse Banner sensor with CANdi for intake detection and a retroreflective Banner/CANdi arrangement at the claw.

### Engineering interpretation

Donor detection is not the same as receiver ownership. A state machine needs to distinguish contact at the pickup, receiver capture and complete clearance before moving the mast. The new sensor reply supplies the missing signal locations; it does not supply exact timeout or debounce settings.

### Transfer and compatibility limits

Transfer centering plus sensor-confirmed direct handoff. A receiving wrist must match the donor pose, not merely be capable of holding coral.

### Unknowns

Exact contact overlap, allowable incoming tube poses and source code transfer timeout remain unknown.

### Proposed validation, not performed

First inspect the missing source interface or CAD; only then test the specific capture/transfer failure that could change the architecture. No hardware experiment was performed in this upgrade.

## Four-stage elevator, rotating shoulder and A-frame

### Published construction

A shoulder-supported continuous lift uses internal HTD belts and extended-stage interlocking stops. The binder gives one X60 lift motor, 6.875:1 and two 18-mm belts.

### Team rationale / attribution boundary

Read cited historical note for team rationale; the operating reconstruction below is editorial and does not establish additional team intent.

### Editorial operating reconstruction

After handoff, shoulder rotation and lift extension move the piece into scoring position. Stops stiffen fully extended stages; during partial extension the guide overlap and bearings carry the moving load.

### Engineering interpretation

The load runs from end effector through carriage and stage guides into shoulder bearings, A-frame and chassis. Stops do not eliminate bending at intermediate heights. Shoulder motion also shifts the moving center of mass and changes cable travel.

### Transfer and compatibility limits

The compact lift and front/back workspace may transfer. Full mast sweep, power cable bend radius and shared climb loads must be rechecked for the new piece.

## Differential orientation with separate piece rollers

### Published construction

Printed bevel gears combine paired wrist drives; the source gives 61.6:1 per drive and #25H output chain. Separate roller drives handle the piece.

### Team rationale / attribution boundary

Read cited historical note for team rationale; the operating reconstruction below is editorial and does not establish additional team intent.

### Editorial operating reconstruction

Two motor coordinates set wrist orientation. Retained coral can then be rolled or ejected; front pinch contacts manage algae. Receiver detection should remain valid through the move or trigger recovery.

### Engineering interpretation

Sharing two motors across two output motions couples available speed and torque. Independently driving piece rollers does not remove that coupling in the orientation transmission. Bearings and gear alignment must hold under piece and tool loads.

### Transfer and compatibility limits

## Algae contacts and shared-joint cage support

### Published construction

Separate algae pickup contacts share an axis with the coral mechanism. Cage capture, passive latches and a sliding support cooperate with the shoulder; the algae intake supplies a support contact.

### Team rationale / attribution boundary

Read cited historical note for team rationale; the operating reconstruction below is editorial and does not establish additional team intent.

### Editorial operating reconstruction

Acquire algae through its own contacts and hand it to the claw. For climb, capture the cage, establish support, then use the shoulder to raise the chassis. The reaction points change as the cage moves.

### Engineering interpretation

A shared axis does not make the two pickups interchangeable. In climb, the intake can become a structural reaction point and must carry a different load from ordinary ball contact. A damaged pickup may therefore remove endgame capability.

### Transfer and compatibility limits

Transfer separate contacts for separate pieces; do not delete the algae assembly while claiming to preserve the complete climb. Any pneumatic historical detail needs an explicit electric redesign under 1833 policy.

### Unknowns

Exact latch release, power-off retention, cage-contact geometry and fault recovery are unresolved.

physical_studies.packaging: The ground pickup spans the front of the base. Coral and algae mechanisms share an axis but have distinct contacts and drives. A central shoulder turns a four-stage elevator supported by an A-frame tied into the base; the carriage carries a compact differential wrist and two-piece end effector. The elevator changes both height and fore-aft position because its whole mast pivots. High scoring therefore sweeps a volume above and across the base, while ground intake deployment occupies the front. The base uses different module clearances fore and aft. Published stage and shoulder renders establish subassembly construction, but battery location, complete wire routing and removal operations remain incomplete.
physical_studies.piece_flow: For coral, floor rollers catch and center the tube, then lift it into a direct handoff. The receiving end effector must be positioned before the donor releases its constraint. The elevator/shoulder move the retained tube to height; the differential reorients it while separate rollers manage placement and release. Algae follows its own intake contacts into the shared end effector, or is acquired from the reef. Climbing changes the force path: cage capture and support contacts allow the shoulder to lift the chassis rather than just a piece.

source_review.whole_robot_explanation: The retained AURELIA architecture combines floor coral acquisition, an independent algae route and a shoulder that rotates an entire four-stage lift. The front end hands the pipe directly to a wrist, then the shoulder and extension choose the scoring position. A distinct lower-task route lets the robot contribute after partners fill the upper branches. The same shoulder takes a very different load when the cage capture supports the chassis.
piece_flow: Floor coral is centered between roller contacts and carried into the receiving wrist. Separate sensing at the collector and claw distinguishes arrival from capture.
The rotating mast, elevator extension and differential wrist place coral toward either scoring side. Older team rationale links the lower mechanisms to horizontal L1 packing.
Separate algae contacts feed the shared end effector or service ground tasks. For endgame the powered capture and shoulder change the load path.
source_review.packaging_and_motion: The mast sweep includes both rotation and extension. Stage overlap and end stops carry different loads at partial and full extension. The intake and nearby algae mechanism also sweep in front of the base, so handoff needs explicit donor and receiver poses and safe recovery at their intersection.

subsystems.name: Coral and algae floor hardware
subsystems.construction: Retained binder describes flex upper contacts, grippy lower roller and independent algae contacts on a shared axis.
subsystems.operation: Gather coral, bring it to the wrist, confirm receiver possession and clear before rotating the mast.
subsystems.team_rationale: Retained team reply connects lower architecture to horizontal L1 packing.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: A large acquisition window is useful only if pieces stay constrained during the direct handoff. Independent sensors reduce ambiguity but require a recovery for disagreement.
subsystems.interfaces: The donor and wrist both control pipe pose near the same point. Algae and coral contacts share package space.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Test a pipe caught by the donor with receiver empty, and test L1 placement in a partially filled trough.
subsystems.unknowns: Measured approach window, timeout and compression tolerance.

subsystems.name: Tilting lift and wrist
subsystems.construction: Retained binder describes shoulder A-frame, continuous internal belts, interlocking stage stops and bevel differential with separate piece rollers.
subsystems.operation: Pivot and extend to set height and side, then orient and release the piece.
subsystems.team_rationale: Prior dossier associates the short stages with stowed envelope and two-sided scoring.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Support loads migrate from guides to stops as stages extend. Wrist speed and torque limits couple when both orientation axes move, regardless of roller independence.
subsystems.interfaces: Camera/target choice, mast sweep and wrist approach must agree with the selected side.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Measure tip error at partial extension and inspect gear backlash after reef contact. Test interruption mid-handoff before allowing the shoulder to move.
subsystems.unknowns: Full belt routing, drive mixing and actual recovery logic.

subsystems.name: Cage capture
subsystems.construction: Powered backpack capture and intake-assisted support in the older account.
